extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of mathematics; mathematicians interested in foundations and the epistemology of proof
extracted.subtask_description: A compact rubric for evaluating mathematical proofs from the perspective of Wittgenstein's later philosophy: emphasis on surveyability, concept-formation, public rule-following, and operational testability. Intended to guide judgments about what counts as a genuine mathematical proof rather than mere calculation or inductive assurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveyability (Übersichtlichkeit)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof must be surveyable: one must be able to grasp it as a unified, finite construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveyability is an epistemic requirement: if a proof is too long to be grasped as a whole it fails Wittgenstein's test and becomes an inductive promise. Machine-checked or massively long proofs (e.g., four-color theorem, Kepler conjecture) may be correct yet lack the epistemic status of a surveyable proof. Evaluation should ask whether a competent reader can hold the proof's structure and main moves in mind as a single object; score higher for proofs that are graspable as a unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept-Forming Function
rubrics_metrics.description: "A proof alters the grammar of a proposition." A genuine proof fixes or reshapes the meanings of the terms used by placing them in new relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the proof does conceptual work (introduces or sharpens concepts) rather than merely deriving a fact using pre-existing vocabulary. The best proofs change how we understand the concepts involved; routine derivations that leave concepts unchanged are at best calculations. Rubric questions: what concepts did this proof reshape? Does the proof change the 'grammar' of the subject?

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule-Following / Algorithmic Determinacy
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical proof must demonstrate that rules generate consequences through finite, algorithmic steps; each step should, in principle, be checkable mechanically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vagueness in inferential moves signals incompleteness rather than depth; every inferential step should be publicly rule-followable by any competent reader applying the same rules. Score proofs higher that make their procedures explicit or spell out how implicit steps follow from public rules; penalize proofs that depend on private or idiosyncratic moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decidability Criterion (method-based problemhood)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Only where there's a method of solution is there a [mathematical] problem." A well-formed mathematical problem must come with an effective/testable method of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat purported problems or proofs that lack an operational decision procedure with suspicion. The rubric favors problems with clear operational success criteria and proofs that exhibit methods for resolving the problem. Score lower for arguments that claim to settle a question without exhibiting a method or test for success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of infinitary intuitions (finitary cashing-out)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should not rely on infinitary intuitions that cannot be cashed out in finite calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittgensteinian evaluation disfavors appeals to infinite processes or intuitions that lack a finite, public formulation. Proofs should offer finite procedures or explain how infinitary reasoning is to be made finite and public; otherwise they fail the requirement of rule-followable, checkable steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveyable scaffolding for long proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Long proofs must provide a surveyable architecture: decomposable lemmas, an overall plan, or other scaffolding that makes the whole graspable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A long proof can be acceptable if it is decomposed into independently graspable lemmas, if its overall plan is surveyable, or if a trained reader can see the architecture without reading every line. The rubric places a burden on long proofs to supply this scaffolding; evaluate whether the decomposition and the statement of the plan render the proof surveyable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicness/spell-outability of implicit detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit steps or details must be, in principle, spellable out in public rules; the ability to 'spell out implicit detail' is required for a complete proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following the tension with Avigad noted in the entry, evaluate whether implicit details are merely tacit or whether they can be articulated as public rules or methods. Penalize arguments that rely on unstated, unspelled rules that only the author understands; reward proofs where implicit moves can be rendered explicit and checked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-patterns to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Common failures: relying on 'intuition' that cannot be made into a public rule; claiming to settle a question without exhibiting a method; producing long manipulations that leave concepts unchanged; presenting proofs too long to survey without compensating structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this list as negative criteria when assessing proofs. Each anti-pattern indicates a serious shortcoming under Wittgenstein's rubric: private appeals to intuition (private rule-following), lack of an operational method, conceptual stagnation (mere calculation), and absence of surveyable structure. Downgrade proofs exhibiting these features unless they are remedied by explicit methods, concept-formation, or surveyable scaffolding.
